items.title: Phoneme-Level Mispronunciation Screening in Polish-Speaking Children with an Explainable Assistant
items.authors: Milosz Dudek(AGH University of Krakow; SoftServe); Daria Hemmerling(AGH University of Krakow; SoftServe); Kamil Kwarciak(AGH University of Krakow; SoftServe); Maciej Stroinski(SoftServe); Maria Pensko(SoftServe); Mateusz Kowalewski(SoftServe); Leonid Pavlovskyi(SoftServe); Sebastian Jurczak(SoftServe); Anna-Mariia Vitkovska(SoftServe); Zuzanna Miodonska(Silesian University of Technology); Natalia Mocko(University of Silesia Katowice); Michal Krecichwost(Silesian University of Technology)
items.abstract: Early identification of speech sound errors in children is often limited by access to specialists, motivating lightweight screening tools that can operate outside the clinic. We present a screening pipeline for Polish-speaking children focused on sibilant substitutions, coupling a wav2vec2-based CTC token recognizer with alignment-based error typing and a template-grounded caregiver assistant (screening, not diagnosis). On a held-out test set of 10 unseen children (559 utterances), the recognizer achieves 88.7% exact sequence match. As a conservative screening proxy, we flag a mismatch when the system emits substitution-evidence (bracketed) tokens at the target segment, yielding 72.9% precision, 61.4% recall (F1=0.67) and a 2.7% false-alarm rate (FPR on target-correct items). We describe the assistant's safety boundaries and outline a clinician-in-the-loop validation plan for future deployment.

items.title: BabAR: from phoneme recognition to developmental measures of young children's speech production
items.authors: Marvin Lavechin(Université Aix-Marseille); Elika Bergelson(Harvard University); Roger Levy(Massachusetts Institute of Technology)
items.abstract: Studying early speech development at scale requires automatic tools, yet automatic phoneme recognition, especially for young children, remains largely unsolved. Building on decades of data collection, we curate TinyVox, a corpus of more than half a million phonetically transcribed child vocalizations in English, French, Portuguese, German, and Spanish. We use TinyVox to train BabAR, a cross-linguistic phoneme recognition system for child speech. We find that pretraining the system on multilingual child-centered daylong recordings substantially outperforms alternatives, and that providing 20 seconds of surrounding audio context during fine-tuning further improves performance. Error analyses show that substitutions predominantly fall within the same broad phonetic categories, suggesting suitability for coarse-grained developmental analyses. We validate BabAR by showing that its automatic measures of speech maturity align with developmental estimates from the literature.

items.title: How does children's pronunciation develop? Capturing syllabic change with children's growth using unsupervised syllable discovery
items.authors: Koharu Horii(NTT, Inc.); Naohiro Tawara(NTT, Inc.); Atsunori Ogawa(NTT, Inc.); Shoko Araki(NTT, Inc.)
items.abstract: Understanding children's pronunciation development is crucial for both speech science and robust automatic speech recognition (ASR) for children. However, conventional ASR-based top-down analyses forcibly map highly variable child speech onto adult-defined phoneme categories, limiting the capture of child-specific and intermediate pronunciations. We propose a bottom-up framework analyzing children's developmental pronunciation variation using an unsupervised syllable discovery (USD) model, Sylber, to objectively verify how their speech converges toward a standard style. Analyzing 957 children aged 5-15, we reveal a clear developmental pattern: expansion of syllable patterns (ages 5-8), followed by gradual stabilization toward adult-like speech. This approach captures fine-grained changes in pronunciation repertoire and stability difficult to observe via top-down methods, demonstrating USD as an effective tool for investigating child speech development at scale.

items.title: Talker Discrimination and Identification in 7-12-year-old Children: Effects of Talker Gender and Phonological Ability
items.authors: Rebecca Holt(Macquarie University); Parisa McGirr(Macquarie University); Chi Yhun Lo(Macquarie University); Anita Szakay(Macquarie University)
items.abstract: Processing talker information is crucial for speech comprehension. Talker discrimination and identification develop over childhood but may be challenging for some clinical populations of children, affecting communication and quality of life. To support future work in clinical populations, this study addressed three open questions about talker processing in typically-developing children aged 7–12, using a novel paradigm to assess talker identification. We asked whether children process pairs of female vs pairs of male voices similarly, to what extent discrimination and identification performance correlate and whether phonological skills predict children’s performance. Children showed similar accuracy for male and female talker pairs. Discrimination and identification were moderately-to-strongly correlated. Phonological working memory predicted identification accuracy. These findings validate our talker identification paradigm and will facilitate future research in clinical populations.

items.title: Robust Multi-Tier Infant-Centered Audio Understanding with Whisper via Structured Speaker Conditioning
items.authors: Xulin Fan(University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign); Jialu Li(University of Arizona); Mohammad Nur Hossain Khan(Worcester Polytechnic Institute); Kexin Hu(University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign); Bashima Islam(Worcester Polytechnic Institute); Mark Hasegawa-Johnson(University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign); Nancy L. McElwain(University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign)
items.abstract: Recent advances in model design and self-supervised audio representations have improved speech and audio understanding, yet infant-centered naturalistic recordings remain challenging due to limited labeled data, low signal-to-noise ratio, and cross-family domain shifts. We present a family-conditioned, multi-tier audio tagger that combines a LoRA-finetuned Whisper encoder with a lightweight, target-speaker-aware Transformer for long-context inference and framewise prediction across tiers. To improve temporal coherence, we incorporate a simple sequence-level smoothing loss, and to enhance robustness across households, we introduce a factorized speaker-token design with a shared tier token and a learned family-specific offset, reducing family bias and promoting generalizable representations. Together, these choices enable efficient and effective infant-centered audio tagging of daylong audio recordings in home environments.

items.title: Advancing Infant Distress Detection: Two- and Three-Way Classification in Real-World Audio Environments
items.authors: Yashaswi Galhotra(University of Texas at Austin); Priyanka Khante(University of Texas at Austin); Anna Madden-Rusnak(UT Austin Dell Medical School); Kaya de Barbaro(University of Texas at Austin)
items.abstract: Infant distress vocalizations, including crying and fussing, function as graded signals that communicate infants needs to caregivers. Most prior distress classifiers are trained on controlled data and fail to generalize to noisier everyday recordings. However, models trained on real-world data show lower accuracy (F1 = 0.61-0.66) and no published models or public datasets distinguish graded fuss vs. cry vocalizations in real-world recordings. Binary classifiers collapse distinct distress states, discarding information needed to model caregiver responses that vary with distress level. We relabel an existing real-world corpus to release the first dataset annotated for cry, fuss, and non-distress from continuous daylong child-worn audio, and establish new benchmarks: our best binary classifier achieves macro F1 = 0.803 and our ternary classifier 0.624. Cross-dataset tests show lab-trained models fail in real-world conditions, whereas ours generalize more robustly.

items.title: BabyHuBERT: Multilingual Self-Supervised Learning for Segmenting Speakers in Child-Centered Long-Form Recordings
items.authors: Théo Charlot(PSL University); Tarek Kunze(PSL University); Maxime Poli(PSL University); Alejandrina Cristia(PSL University); Emmanuel Dupoux(PSL University); Marvin Lavechin(Université Aix-Marseille)
items.abstract: Child-centered daylong recordings are essential for studying early language development, but existing speech models trained on clean adult data perform poorly due to acoustic and linguistic differences. We introduce BabyHuBERT, a self-supervised speech model trained on 13,000 hours of multilingual child-centered recordings from 40+ languages. Evaluated on voice type classification, the task of identifying who produces speech and when in child-centered recordings (key child, other children, male, and female adults), BabyHuBERT-VTC achieves F1-scores from 55.0% to 76.1% across six corpora, consistently outperforming W2V2-LL4300 and HuBERT (pretrained on English daylongs and clean adult speech, respectively). Notable gains include 14.0 and 18.3 absolute F1 points over HuBERT on Vanuatu and Solomon Islands, demonstrating effectiveness on underrepresented languages. We share code and models to support researchers working with child-centered recordings across diverse linguistic contexts.

items.title: Context-aware child-directed speech detection from long-form recordings
items.authors: Théo Charlot(PSL University); Tarek Kunze(PSL University); Kaveri K. Sheth(PSL University); Alejandrina Cristia(PSL University); Marvin Lavechin(Université Aix-Marseille)
items.abstract: Automatically distinguishing child-directed speech from adult-directed speech in long-form recordings is key to scalable analyses of children's language environments. Existing approaches process utterances in isolation and have been evaluated primarily on English. We address these gaps along three dimensions. First, we fine-tune and evaluate six-self supervised models on a multilingual dataset of 182 children, showing that in-domain pre-training on child-centered recordings substantially outperforms models trained on adult speech. Second, we demonstrate that incorporating surrounding context substantially improves classification, with an absolute gain of 13.8% in average F1-score. Third, we evaluate our model in a realistic end-to-end pipeline, from adult speech detection to addressee classification, showing that performance drops under automatic segmentation but still consistently outperforms a rule-based baseline.

items.title: Benchmarking Adult Addressee Classification Across Child- and Adult- Directed Speech Datasets
Deriving Benchmarking Datasets from Long-Form Recordings: Challenges and Opportunities
items.authors: Kaveri K. Sheth(PSL University); Lawrence Borst(PSL University); Tarek Kunze(PSL University); Marvin Lavechin(Université Aix-Marseille); Okko Räsänen(Tampere University); Sho Tsuji(PSL University); Loann Peurey(PSL University); Alix Bourree(PSL University); Alejandrina Cristia(PSL University)
items.abstract: Long-form recordings (LFRs) of child-centered audio are ecologically valid sources for studying early language development, but three problems limit their use. First, LFR corpora are collected across sites with heterogeneous formats and consent structures, making cross-corpus use non-trivial. Second, without standardized benchmarks, assessing whether tools generalize across languages and conditions is hard. Third, ML workflows rarely respect privacy constraints governing sensitive child speech. This paper presents a framework addressing all three: a standardized collection of 27 child-centered datasets built with open-source tools (S1); a replicable pipeline for four speech-processing benchmarks (S2); and ELSI, a role-based ecosystem embedding ethical governance into the ML workflow (S3). We demonstrate the framework via a voice type classification case study and show the three solutions are mutually dependent.

items.title: Measuring English and Vietnamese language input and output in an Australian preschool – A longitudinal study
items.authors: Ha Chi Tran(Western Sydney University.); Minh Anh Tran(Western Sydney University.); Mai Linh Tran(Deakin University.); Weicong Li(Western Sydney University.); Paola Escudero(Western Sydney University.)
items.abstract: Providing heritage language (HL) support to enable bilingualism from an early age, especially within the community and outside the home environment, is important. However, in Australia, there is limited support for maintaining HL in early childhood education. In this study, we measured English and Vietnamese as HL input and output in a Vietnamese language exposure program in Melbourne, Australia. We compared the duration of utterances produced in the first eight sessions of two implementations of the program. An increase in children's total speech from the first to the second implementation indicates greater engagement and participation. The results demonstrate that English remained the dominant language in both implementations. Regarding Vietnamese, children's output increased while the input given by the facilitator reduced. By comparing two implementations, this study offers a refined quantitative methodology for measuring language input and output in a language program designed for preschoolers. The implications of this study support the implementation of similar programs in Vietnamese and other HL in Australia and worldwide.

items.title: Dynamic Time Warping Reveals Prosodic Alignment in Caregiver–Child Interactions across Languages
items.authors: Olivier Rüst(University of Zürich); Sabine Stoll(University of Zürich)
items.abstract: The distinctive properties of child-directed (CDS) and contingent caregiver speech, compared to child-surrounding speech, are well documented, yet their underlying mechanisms remain unclear. We investigate how prosodic patterns in contingent CDS emerge from caregiver-child interaction, focusing on pitch-contour similarity. In longitudinal, naturalistic language acquisition corpora of English, Japanese, and Russian, we quantify acoustic similarity via Dynamic Time Warping and model its relation to temporal proximity between turns and child age. Bayesian mixed-effects analyses reveal greater pitch-contour similarity for temporally adjacent utterances and decreasing similarity with increasing child age, consistent with social accommodation effects. Our results suggest that key acoustic properties of CDS may partly arise from general interactional processes between caregivers and children such as accommodation but can be modulated by culture and language specific norms and grammar.

items.title: Entropy-Aware Domain-Routed Mixture-of-Experts Speech-LLM Framework: A Case Study of Multi-Domain Child-Adult ASR
items.authors: Mohan Shi(University of California); Kaiyuan Zhang(University of California); Zilai Wang(University of California); Natarajan Balaji Shankar(University of California); Eray Eren(University of California, Los Angeles); Abeer Alwan(University of California, Los Angeles)
items.abstract: While Speech Large Language Models (Speech-LLMs)have achieved strong performance on adult Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), their effectiveness on child speech remains under-explored, and single models often struggle to handle diverse adult and child age groups simultaneously. This paper proposes a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Speech-LLM for unified ASR across adult and child speech spanning diverse environments and age groups. The framework employs a Classifier-based Domain Router (C-DR) with a coarse-to-fine strategy and integrates both a Mixture-of-Projectors (MoP) and a Mixture-of-LoRAs (MoL) to model domain-specific variations. To address routing uncertainty near domain boundaries, an Entropy-Aware Routing (EAR) mechanism is introduced to dynamically incorporate a shared expert. Experiments on public child corpora demonstrate consistent improvements over baselines while preserving adult ASR performance. To our knowledge, this is the first work leveraging Speech-LLMs for unified, multi-domain ASR encompassing both children and adults.

title: Diphthongs and Monophthongs
header: Wednesday 30 September 2026 - 16:30-18:30 - Area 2 - Oral 3 - Diphthongs and Monophthongs

items.title: On the challenges and benefits of dynamic vowel analyses
items.abstract: The aim of this presentation is to give an overview of recent studies dealing with the dynamics of monophthongs, diphthongs, and hiatus sequences. Traditionally, monophthongs have been defined by their steady states, but especially in continuous and non-laboratory speech, steady states are often hard to identify given increased articulatory blending. Vowel-vowel-sequences, on the other hand, have long been recognized as inherently dynamic, but for reasons of complexity reduction and computational efficiency, they are still often analyzed in terms of static metrics such as DCT coefficients or the rate of change of the formants. In this presentation, I will show how novel methodological approaches to dynamic analyses can provide new insights into vowels and vowel sequences, but also discuss under which circumstances a more straight-forward, static analysis suffices.

items.title: Phonetic evidence for contrastive length in Nakanamanga monophthongs
items.authors: Shubo Li(Australian National University)
items.abstract: This paper presents the first acoustic phonetic investigation of contrastive vowel length in Nakanamanga, an Oceanic language of Vanuatu. Previous research has been unclear about whether vowel length is contrastive, and if it applies to all five vowel qualities. In addition, the status of vowel length in languages of central Vanuatu in general remains unclear. Recent phonological analyses argue for a length contrast across all vowel qualities based on minimal pairs, but the durational characteristics of Nakanamanga monophthongs have not yet been examined. This study investigates if vowel duration provides phonetic evidence for the proposed phonological contrast. Results show that long and short monophthongs differ significantly in duration across all vowel qualities, with long vowels averaging 2.08 times the length of short vowels. The findings provide clear acoustic support for a phonological vowel length contrast in Nakanamanga.

items.title: To glide or not to glide: Acoustic realization of the diphthong-hiatus contrast in Italian and Romanian
items.authors: Johanna Cronenberg(Université Paris Cité; LPP; CNRS); Lori Lamel(CNRS; Université Paris-Saclay; LISN); Ioana Chitoran(LLF; Université Paris Cité; IUF; CNRS)
items.abstract: Vowel sequences such as /ia/ can be produced and categorized either as a monosyllabic diphthong /ja/ or as a heterosyllabic hiatus /i.a/. In order to study whether lexical stress and position within word facilitate or block glide formation, we analyzed the duration and formant dynamics of /ia/ in large corpora of Italian and Romanian. In line with their respective phonological categorization of /ia/, Italian speakers produced shorter and slightly shallower formant trajectories than Romanian speakers, who generally tended to produce more hiatus-like formants. In Italian, gliding seemed to be blocked when the vowel sequence was stressed, while gliding was preferred in Romanian only for unstressed medial /ia/. At the same time, there was a lot of overlap between the two languages, indicating that the diphthong-hiatus contrast may be gradient both across and within languages. Thus, this study provides the basis for future investigations of the perceptual categorization of /ia/.

items.title: Modelling diphthong dynamics: A GAMM-based analysis of Australian English diphthongs
items.authors: Ksenia Gnevsheva(Australian National University); Canaan Lan(University of Melbourne); Gerard Docherty(Griffith University); Catherine Travis(Australian National University)
items.abstract: Diphthongs are inherently dynamic segments, yet they are typically analysed using discrete time points, reducing their complex trajectories to static onset and offset targets. In this study, we adopt a fully dynamic modelling approach using Generalised Additive Mixed Models to analyse formant movement across the entire vowel trajectory of five Australian English diphthongs, and conduct comparisons across gender and location. Data come from two spontaneous speech corpora collected in one urban and one regional location and prepared following comparable protocols. Statistical analysis reveals an effect of gender for all vowels, and location for three vowels, with women and urban speakers being ahead in the change. Importantly, some differences emerged at points other than the onset and offset, or were more clearly captured when the full trajectory was modelled, underscoring the value of a trajectory-based approach to diphthong analysis.

items.title: Variation and change in dynamicity of Australian English diphthongs in Sydney
items.authors: Benjamin Purser(Australian National University)
items.abstract: Diphthongs are established loci of variation and change in Australian English, yet have been analysed predominantly using static vowel measures. More recent research exploring dynamicity of these vowels indicates a degree of variation and change over time in their dynamic properties, however this prior work has generally considered F1 and F2 separately. This paper examines dynamicity of F1 and F2 simultaneously using multivariate functional principal component analysis (MFPCA), analysing more than 57,000 tokens of six diphthongs (FACE, FLEECE, GOAT, NEAR, MOUTH, and PRICE) from a corpus of spontaneous speech, and considering both linguistic and social conditioning (according to age, gender, and social class). Overall patterns of social variation align with prior research about the expected direction of change for each vowel, yet considering F1 and F2 in tandem provides a more holistic understanding of the dynamic properties of these diphthongs.

title: Speaker Identity, States, and Traits in Paralinguistics
header: Wednesday 30 September 2026 - 16:30-18:30 - Area 3 - Oral 4 - Speaker Identity, States, and Traits in Paralinguistics

items.title: Audio-Based Understanding of Audiobook Narration Appeal
items.authors: Shahar Elisha(Spotify; Queen Mary University of London); Mariano Beguerisse-Díaz(Spotify); Emmanouil Benetos(Queen Mary University of London)
items.abstract: Narration is central to the audiobook listening experience, shaping how listeners engage with and understand the content. This work explores how narration qualities shape an audiobook's appeal, noting that their effects can vary by genre, title, and audience. We extract vocal and acoustic features (e.g., tone, pace, loudness) from LibriVox using pre-trained audio models and analyse their relationship with consumption data (specifically, view-rate) and their interplay with genre and title. Despite limited consumption data, we find that acoustic information alone has a robust association with appeal, even after accounting for title effects. We further validate these findings using more nuanced proprietary engagement metrics. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic computational study linking narration qualities, genre, title, and audiobook consumption, highlighting the potential of data-driven insights to improve audiobook personalisation and narrator casting.

items.title: The SSPNet Speaker Personality Corpus Version 2: Investigating the Role of Language Understanding in Automatic Personality Perception
items.authors: Nisreen Alshubaily(University of Glasgow; Imam Mohammad Ibn Saud Islamic University); Emily O'Hara(University of Glasgow); Tanaya Guha(University of Glasgow); Alessandro Vinciarelli(University of Glasgow)
items.abstract: This article presents the SSPNet Speaker Personality Corpus Version 2 - an enhanced edition of the SSPNet Speaker Personality Corpus, the most widely used public benchmark for speech-based Automatic Personality Perception. The main improvements are: (1) all speech samples are fully transcribed (the original corpus included only audio); (2) personality annotations use a 100-point scale (instead of the original 9-point scale); and (3) the corpus includes two rater groups: one that understands the language of the recordings and one that does not. These enhancements enable multimodal approaches (previously not possible with the original), facilitate regression methodologies (hindered by the coarse 9-point scale), and support investigations into how language comprehension affects personality perception (previously infeasible). The release also provides unimodal and multimodal baselines with reproducible experimental protocols: SPC V2 Repository.

items.title: Learning speaker identities in dialogue: Conversational familiarisation modulates response bias and confidence in voice recognition
items.authors: Tianze Xu(University of Zurich); Volker Dellwo(University of Zurich)
items.abstract: In everyday communication, voice learning occurs in conversational dialogue, yet most experimental research relies on isolated, explicitly memorised speech. We examined how conversational familiarisation and attentional focus influence subsequent voice recognition. Two hundred English-speaking participants listened either to a coherent four-speaker dialogue or to a scrambled version and were instructed to attend to speaker identity, speech content, or simply listen without a specific focus. Participants then completed a voice recognition (old/new) task. Results revealed no main effects of stimulus type or focus. Critically, familiarisation stimulus interacted with ground truth: dialogue familiarisation increased recognition of old speakers and confidence in those responses, but also increased incorrect endorsements of new speakers as old, suggesting a shift in response bias. These findings demonstrate how conversational context systematically modulates voice recognition decisions.

items.title: Speaker-Filtered Heterogeneous Graph Network: Toward Privacy-Preserving Multimodal Emotion Recognition
items.authors: heying song(Tianjin Normal University); Jing Han(Hunan University; Yuelushan Center for Industrial Innovation); Yandi Zheng(Tianjin Normal University); Zixing Zhang(Hunan University); Ziping Zhao(Tianjin Normal University); Björn Schuller(Technische Universität München; Imperial College London)
items.abstract: Multimodal Dialogue Emotion Recognition (MDER) plays a role in human-computer interaction, yet existing approaches often rely on global context aggregation that violates speaker privacy and introduces temporal information leakage. We propose Speaker-Filtered Heterogeneous Graph Network (SF-HGN), a privacy-aware framework for multimodal emotion recognition in conversations. SF-HGN restricts graph propagation to single-speaker induced subgraphs to maintain speaker-level privacy, while preserving contextual information through a Context-Aware Graph Injection (CAGI) module. CAGI extracts cross-speaker emotional cues using tri-modal attention within a strict causal window, preventing future information leakage and reducing noisy inter-modal interactions. By combining causal masking, speaker filtering, and heterogeneous graph modeling, SF-HGN enables robust emotion reasoning without exposing non-target speaker features. Experiments on the IEMOCAP and MELD datasets show its effectiveness.

items.title: Hidden Priors in Speech LLMs: Speaker Identity Shapes Emotional Perception
items.authors: Hsing-Hang Chou(National Tsing Hua University); Bo-Hao Su(National Tsing Hua University); Krishna Somandepalli(Google DeepMind); Chi-Chun Lee(National Tsing Hua University)
items.abstract: Speech LLMs enable emotion-aware voice interaction, yet their emotion judgments can be shaped by contextual identity priors beyond the audio signal. We isolate this effect by holding each utterance fixed while varying only prompt-injected speaker descriptors (accent, country, language), across MSP-Podcast and BIIC-Podcast. Across multiple speech LLMs, identity text alone yields statistically reliable performance disparities, measured as the spread between best- and worst-performing identity conditions, indicating systematic shifts in emotion prediction. Saliency analysis shows that identity-driven prediction transitions often co-occur with larger changes in acoustic focus over the audio-token span, suggesting altered reliance on speech evidence. To reduce this sensitivity, we apply a lightweight LoRA adapter with two prompt strategies. Overall, we provide a prompt-controlled framework to quantify, interpret, and reduce identity-conditioned sensitivity in speech LLM emotion perception.

items.title: What Makes Synthetic Speech Sound Sarcastic? A Prosody-Controlled Perception Study
items.authors: Zhu Li(University of Groningen); Shekhar Nayak(University of Groningen); Matt Coler(University of Groningen)
items.abstract: Prosody plays an important role in sarcasm perception, yet previous studies have relied on naturally produced speech that lacks fine-grained control over individual acoustic dimensions. As prosodic cues co-vary in natural data, isolating their independent contributions remains challenging. We introduce a controlled framework using neural text-to-speech (TTS) with prompt-based prosodic conditioning to manipulate speech rate, pitch variation, and loudness. An orthogonal stimulus set was constructed to enable causal testing of prosodic cue effects. Human listeners rated sarcasm and naturalness, and their judgments were compared with predictions from a foundation model capable of processing audio input. Results show that loudness primarily drives human sarcasm perception, whereas the model assigns greater weight to speech rate, indicating limited behavioral alignment. This study shows how controllable neural TTS enables investigation of prosodic cue weighting in speech perception.

title: Speech Deepfake Detection, Attribution and Characterization
header: Wednesday 30 September 2026 - 16:30-18:30 - Area 4 - Oral 9 - Speech Deepfake Detection, Attribution and Characterization

items.title: Bridging the Age Gap: Towards Detecting Neural Audio Codec Synthesized Elderly Speech Deepfake
items.authors: Orchid Chetia Phukan(NTHU); Girish (UPES); Mohd Mujtaba Akhtar(VBSPU); Chi-Chun Lee(NTHU)
items.abstract: In this study, we introduce the Elderly CodecFake Detection (ECFD) task and release the Elderly-CodecFake (ECF) dataset in English and Chinese. We show that state-of-the-art CF detectors trained on previous benchmark CF datasets generalize poorly to elderly speech, revealing a critical vulnerability. We further hypothesize and demonstrate that multimodal foundation models (FMs) such as LanguageBind (LB) and ImageBind (IB) are more effective for ECFD due to their exposure to elderly content during cross-modal pretraining. Motivated by prior evidence that fusion of FMs enhances downstream performance, we explore fusion of FMs for ECFD. To this end, we propose BONSAI, a novel framework that employs Jensen-Shannon Divergence as the fusion mechanism. BONSAI with the fusion of LB and IB achieves an average EER (%) of 1.66 and outperforms individual FMs as well as competitive SOTA baselines, establishing a new benchmark for the ECFD task.

items.title: DGS-MLDG: Domain Gradient Surgery Guided Meta-Learning for Domain Generalization in Speech Deepfake Detection
items.authors: Siqing QIN(Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Kong Aik LEE(Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Youzhi TU(Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Eng Siong Chng(Nanyang Technological University); Man-Wai Mak(Hong Kong Polytechnic University)
items.abstract: Speech deepfake detection faces significant challenges due to domain shifts. Domain generalization (DG), particularly meta-learning for domain generalization (MLDG), offers a promising solution by simulating and mitigating domain shifts. However, MLDG is often hindered by conflicting gradients between its meta-train and meta-test objectives, leading to suboptimal performance. To address this problem, we propose domain gradient surgery (DGS), a meta-learning method that resolves conflicts through an asymmetric projection strategy. DGS removes the destructive component from the meta-test gradient, ensuring a conflict-free optimization trajectory versus the meta-train gradient. Furthermore, we introduce layer-wise DGS (LW-DGS), an efficient variant of DGS that dynamically identifies and intervenes only conflict-prone layers. Extensive experiments on challenging benchmarks demonstrate that DGS-MLDG and LW-DGS-MLDG achieve an average relative EER reduction of 5.29% and 4.04%, respectively.

items.title: Does Fine-tuning by Reinforcement Learning Improve Generalization in Binary Speech Deepfake Detection?
items.authors: Xin Wang(National Institute of Informatics); Wanying Ge(National Institute of Informatics); Junichi Yamagishi(National Institute of Informatics)
items.abstract: Building speech deepfake detection models that are generalizable to unseen attacks remains a challenging problem. Although the field has shifted toward a pre-training and fine-tuning paradigm using speech foundation models, most approaches rely solely on supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Inspired by the field of large language models, wherein reinforcement learning (RL) is used for model fine-tuning, we investigate the impact of RL, specifically Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). The results from experiments using multiple detectors and test sets indicate that pure GRPO-based fine-tuning improves performance on out-of-domain test sets while maintaining performance on target-domain test data. This approach outperforms both SFT-only and hybrid setups. Our ablation studies further suggest that the negative reward in GRPO may be a key factor in this improvement.

items.title: Domain-Adaptive Dual-Gating Mixture of Experts for Generalizable Speech Deepfake Detection
items.authors: Siqing Qin(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Zhe Li(The University of Hong Kong); Kong Aik Lee(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Man-Wai Mak(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University)
items.abstract: Recent advances in speech deepfake detection (SDD) have leveraged the Mixture of Experts (MoE) to enhance generalization capacity. However, existing gating networks often overlook the acoustic and temporal cues of deepfakes. In this work, we propose a novel domain-adaptive dual-gating MoE (DADG-MoE) framework for SDD under unseen attack types and acoustic conditions. Our innovative dual-gating mechanism leverages Sinc-layer-based filters to process both low-level acoustic signals (raw waveforms) and high-level speech representations from a large self-supervised learning (SSL) model. It further incorporates domain prototypes to guide expert routing based on implicit deepfake patterns. The lightweight affine experts process the routed inputs. Experiments show that our DADG-MoE significantly outperforms the baseline, achieving up to a 40.8% relative EER reduction on challenging out-of-dataset benchmarks. This framework demonstrates superior generalization capabilities and efficient design.

items.title: QAMO: Quality-aware Multi-centroid One-class Learning For Speech Deepfake Detection
items.authors: Duc-Tuan Truong(Nanyang Technological University); Tianchi Liu(National University of Singapore); Ruijie Tao(National University of Singapore); Junjie Li(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Kong Aik Lee(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Eng Siong Chng(Nanyang Technological University)
items.abstract: Recent work shows that one-class learning (OCL) can detect unseen deepfake by modeling a compact distribution of bona fide speech around a single centroid. However, OCL can oversimplify the bona fide class distribution and ignore useful cues, such as speech quality, which reflects the naturalness of the speech. Speech quality can be easily estimated via the Mean Opinion Score using assessment models. In this paper, we propose QAMO: Quality-Aware Multi-Centroid One-Class Learning for speech deepfake detection. QAMO improves OCL by introducing multiple quality-aware centroids. Each centroid is optimized to represent distinct speech quality subspaces to better capture the intra-class variability of bona fide speech. In addition, QAMO supports a multi-centroid ensemble scoring strategy that improves decision threshold and removes the need for quality labels at inference. QAMO achieves a 5.21% equal error rate in the In-the-Wild dataset, outperforming prior OCL and quality-aware systems.

items.title: Duration-aware self-attention for speech deepfake detection
items.authors: Youzhi Tu(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Xin Fang(University of Science and Technology of China; iFlytek Co., Ltd.); Liping Chen(University of Science and Technology of China); Zhenhua Ling(University of Science and Technology of China); Kong Aik Lee(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University)
items.abstract: Current speech deepfake detection systems mostly use fixed-length training and evaluation through audio padding or truncation. However, the utterances' durations are inherently variable, which poses a challenge to deepfake detection. To address this limitation, we propose incorporating the timing embeddings computed from the audio duration and the segment offset into self-attention. The objective is to correct the attention bias map when computing the attention coefficients, so that the timing embeddings guide a better learning of positional interactions. The resulting method is called duration-aware self-attention (DASA), which is implemented in three ways. Experiments on ASVspoof21, In-the-Wild, and CodecFake show the effectiveness of the relative positional encoding based DASA. This result indicates that the proposed method is beneficial to alleviate duration variations.

title: Speech and Audio Quality Assessment
header: Wednesday 30 September 2026 - 16:30-18:30 - Area 5 - Oral 3 - Speech and Audio Quality Assessment

items.title: DNSMOS-C: Improving End-to-end Speech Quality Models via Contrastive Learning
items.authors: Xinyu Liang(KTH Royal Institute of Technology); Fredrik Cumlin(KTH Royal Institute of Technology); Victor Ungureanu(Google LLC); Chandan K. A. Reddy(Google LLC); Christian Schüldt(Google LLC); Saikat Chatterjee(KTH Royal Institute of Technology)
items.abstract: We introduce DNSMOS-C, a compact end-to-end speech quality assessment model that extends the DNSMOS Pro framework by integrating a MOS-guided triplet-based contrastive loss. Applied directly to the intermediate embeddings, this contrastive supervision encourages the latent space to be better organized with respect to perceptual quality while preserving the simplicity and efficiency of DNSMOS Pro. Unlike prior methods that depend on large pre-trained self-supervised learning (SSL) encoders and multi-stage training, DNSMOS-C jointly learns speech representations and MOS regression within a single, unified framework. Experiments on multiple datasets show that DNSMOS-C consistently improves correlation metrics over DNSMOS Pro and achieves better generalization on challenging out-of-domain test sets. Furthermore, latent space analyses indicate that our approach learns representations that exhibit an emergent low-dimensional quality ordering, which enhances interpretability and improves training stability. These findings demonstrate that MOS-guided contrastive learning enables more robust and accurate quality predictions without incurring additional computational overhead.

items.title: ANCHOR: Autoregressive Non-intrusive Chunk-Ordered Refinement for Joint Multi-Resolution Speech Quality Modeling
items.authors: Zhuoyan Tao(USC); Jiatong Shi(Carnegie Mellon University); Hye-jin Shim(Carnegie Mellon University); Shinji Watanabe(Carnegie Mellon University)
items.abstract: While speech quality is typically assessed on complete utterances, streaming and generative systems require incremental estimation from partial audio. Existing predictors assume full context, degrading on prefix-constrained inputs. Extending ARECHO, we propose ANCHOR, reformulating incremental assessment as a multi-resolution autoregressive task. It models chunk-and utterance-level quality within a single decoder using dual-resolution tokens and a resolution-aware hierarchy for coarse-to-fine refinement. Experiments show substantial robustness under partial input, including a 48% PLCMOS error reduction on 2-second prefixes. Convergence analysis reveals a 4-6 s effective perceptual context horizon. A stress test further isolates structured extrapolation biases under localized corruption. Results demonstrate that hierarchical supervision improves incremental prediction and elucidates how perceptual quality accumulates over time.

items.title: An Empirical Analysis of Task-Induced Encoder Bias in Fréchet Audio Distance
items.authors: Wonwoo Jeong(Sogang University)
items.abstract: Fréchet Audio Distance (FAD) is the de facto standard for evaluating text-to-audio generation, yet its scores depend on the underlying encoder's embedding space. An encoder's training task dictates which acoustic features are preserved or discarded, causing FAD to inherit systematic task-induced biases. We decompose evaluation into Recall, Precision, and Alignment (split into semantic and structural dimensions), using log-scale normalization for fair cross-encoder comparison. Controlled experiments on six encoders across two datasets reveal a four-axis trade-off: reconstruction-based AudioMAE leads precision sensitivity; ASR-trained Whisper dominates structural detection but is blind to signal degradation; classification-trained VGGish maximizes semantic detection but penalizes legitimate intra-class variation. Since no single encoder is a universal evaluator, future metrics must shift toward evaluation-native encoders intrinsically aligned with human perception.

items.title: PASQA: Pitch-Accent-Focused Speech Quality Assessment Model Trained on Synthetic Speech with Accent Errors
items.authors: Masaya Kawamura(LY Corporation); Yuma Shirahata(LY Corporation); Kentaro Mitsui(LY Corporation); Reo Shimizu(LY Corporation)
items.abstract: Existing mean opinion score (MOS) prediction models typically predict utterance-level naturalness MOS and can be insensitive to localized pitch-accent errors. We propose Pitch-Accent-focused Speech Quality Assessment (PASQA), which explicitly targets pitch-accent correctness. To train our model, we construct a controlled Japanese accent-error dataset by changing accent patterns using an accent-controllable text-to-speech system, and compute a pseudo accent-quality score from the accent-error rate. PASQA builds on self-supervised representations and employs mora-conditioned fusion, ranking loss, an auxiliary accent-error localization task, and speaker-invariant training. Experiments show that conventional models fail to preserve the ordering by accent-error severity, whereas PASQA achieves high ordering accuracy on both seen and unseen speakers. Further, PASQA shows stronger agreement with human accent-correctness judgments. The code is available at https://github.com/lycorp-jp/PASQA.

items.title: URGENT-MOS: Unified Multi-Metric and Preference Learning for Robust Speech Quality Assessment
items.authors: Wei Wang(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Wangyou Zhang(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Chenda Li(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Jiahe Wang(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Samuele Cornell(Carnegie Mellon University); Marvin Sach(Technische Universität Braunschweig); Kohei Saijo(Waseda University); Yihui Fu(Technische Universität Braunschweig); Zhaoheng Ni(Meta AI); Mengxiao Bi(VUI Labs); Tim Fingscheidt(Technische Universität Braunschweig); Shinji Watanabe(Carnegie Mellon University); Yanmin Qian(Shanghai Jiao Tong University)
items.abstract: Automatic speech quality assessment (SQA) is essential for evaluating modern speech generation systems. However, human listening tests are costly and difficult to scale. The URGENT Challenge introduced a multi-metric evaluation protocol that assesses diverse absolute quality metrics, including human Mean Opinion Score (MOS) and objective measures, together with comparative human preference tests. This protocol highlights the need for unified modeling under heterogeneous supervision. Despite this need, most existing approaches focus on either absolute quality prediction or preference prediction. Motivated by the URGENT protocol, we propose URGENT-MOS, a unified SQA framework that jointly models multi-metric absolute quality prediction and pairwise preference prediction within a shared architecture. By leveraging diverse metrics and learning from heterogeneous data, the framework improves performance and cross-domain robustness in both absolute quality and preference prediction tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/vvwangvv/URGENT-MOS.

items.title: Audio Hallucination Attacks: Probing the Reliability of Large Audio Language Models
items.authors: Ashish Seth(University of Maryland); Sonal Kumar(University of Maryland); Ramaneswaran Selvakuma(University of Maryland); Nishit Anand(University of Maryland); Utkarsh Tyagi(University of Maryland); Prem Seetharaman(Adobe Research); Ramani Duraiswami(University of Maryland); Dinesh Manocha(University of Maryland)
items.abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) achieve strong performance on audio-language tasks; however, their reliability in real-world settings remains underexplored. We introduce Audio Hallucination Attacks (AHA), an attack suite called AHA-Eval, comprising 6.5K QA pairs designed to test whether LALMs genuinely ground their responses in the audio input. AHA targets two attack surfaces: (i) query-based attacks, which exploit question structure to induce hallucinations about absent sounds, and (ii) audio-based attacks, which inject synthetic speech describing non-existent events into the audio stream. Evaluating state-of-the-art LALMs, including Audio Flamingo 3 and Gemini 3 Pro, we observe high attack success rates of 95.35% and 79.65%, respectively, revealing a reliability gap that is hidden by standard benchmark performance. To mitigate this, we propose a 120K QA post-alignment dataset, AHA-Guard, which successfully reduces attack success rates by up to 49%.

title: Audio-Visual and Generative Target Speaker Extraction
header: Wednesday 30 September 2026 - 16:30-18:30 - Area 6 - Oral 4 - Audio-Visual and Generative Target Speaker Extraction

items.title: MeanFlow-TSE: One-Step Generative Target Speaker Extraction with Mean Flow
items.authors: Riki Shimizu(Columbia University); Xilin Jiang(Columbia University); Nima Mesgarani(Columbia University)
items.abstract: Target speaker extraction (TSE) aims to isolate a desired speaker‘s voice from a multi-speaker mixture using auxiliary information. Although recent advances in diffusion and flow-matching models have improved TSE performance, these methods typically require multi-step sampling, which limits their practicality in low-latency settings. In this work, we propose MeanFlow-TSE, a one-step generative TSE framework trained with mean-flow objectives, enabling fast and high-quality generation without iterative refinement. Building on the AD-FlowTSE paradigm, our method defines a flow between the background and target source that is governed by the mixing ratio. Experiments on the Libri2Mix corpus show that our approach outperforms existing generative TSE models in separation quality and perceptual metrics while requiring only a single inference step. These results demonstrate that mean-flow-guided one-step generation offers an efficient alternative for real-time target speaker extraction.

items.title: Plug-and-Steer: Decoupling Separation and Selection in Audio-Visual Target Speaker Extraction
items.authors: Doyeop Kwak(Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology); Suyeon Lee(Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology); Joon Son Chung(Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology)
items.abstract: The goal of this paper is to provide a new perspective on audio-visual target speaker extraction (AV-TSE) by decoupling separation and target selection. Conventional AV-TSE systems typically integrate audio and visual features deeply to re-learn the entire separation process, which can act as a fidelity ceiling due to the noisy nature of in-the-wild audio-visual datasets. To address this, we propose Plug-and-Steer, which assigns high-fidelity separation to a frozen audio-only backbone and limits the role of the visual modality strictly to target selection. We introduce the Latent Steering Matrix (LSM), a minimalist linear transformation that re-routes latent features within the backbone to anchor the target speaker to a designated channel. Experiments across four representative architectures show that our method effectively preserves the acoustic priors of diverse backbones, achieving perceptual quality comparable to that of the original backbones. Audio samples are on the demo page.

items.title: Audio-visual Contrastive Alignment for Diffusion-based Visual-conditioned Speech Enhancement
items.authors: Colombe Mboungou(INRIA); Mostafa Sadeghi(INRIA); Jean-Eudes Ayilo(INRIA); Romain Serizel(LORIA; Université de Lorraine)
items.abstract: Audio-visual speech enhancement (AVSE) exploits visual cues such as lip movements to recover speech in noisy environments. Recent work introduced diffusion-based unsupervised AVSE, where a speech diffusion model conditioned on visual features via cross-attention is trained and used as a data-driven prior for posterior sampling-based speech enhancement. Despite promising performance over its audio-only counterpart, the impact of explicitly enforcing cross-modal alignment in the fusion remains unclear. In this work, we propose to augment the diffusion training objective with a contrastive audio–visual loss to encourage stronger use of visual information while keeping the posterior sampling framework unchanged. Experiments across matched and mismatched test data show consistent improvements in interference suppression, signal reconstruction, and perceptual quality, with the largest gains at low SNRs. Code is available at https://github.com/cexauce/AV-CA-DiffUSE.

items.title: GenTSE: Enhancing Target Speaker Extraction via a Coarse-to-Fine Generative Language Model
items.authors: Haoyang Li(Nanyang Technological University); Xuyi Zhuang(Nanyang Technological University); Azmat Adnan(Nanyang Technological University); Ye Ni(Southeast University); Wei Rao(Nanyang Technological University); Shreyas Gopal(Nanyang Technological University); Eng Siong Chng(Nanyang Technological University); Boon Siew Han(Schaeffler); Yuanjin Zheng(Nanyang Technological University)
items.abstract: Language Model (LM)-based generative modeling has emerged as a promising direction for TSE, offering potential for improved generalization and high-fidelity speech. We propose GenTSE, a two-stage decoder-only generative LM for TSE: Stage-1 predicts coarse semantic tokens, and Stage-2 generates fine acoustic tokens. Separating semantics and acoustics stabilizes decoding and yields more accurate target speech. Both stages use continuous SSL or codec embeddings, offering richer context than discretized-prompt methods. To reduce exposure bias, we employ a Frozen-LM Conditioning training strategy that conditions the LMs on predicted tokens from earlier checkpoints to reduce the gap between teacher-forcing training and autoregressive inference. We further apply DPO to better align outputs with perceptual preferences. Experiments on Libri2Mix show that GenTSE surpasses previous LM-based systems in speech quality, intelligibility, and speaker consistency.

items.title: Online Audio-Visual Target Speaker Extraction with Viseme-Guided Lightweight Visual Pretraining
items.authors: Zixuan Li(Inner Mongolia University); Xueliang Zhang(Inner Mongolia University); Lei Miao(Lenovo); Zhipeng Yan(Lenovo); Ying Sun(Lenovo); Chong Zhu(Lenovo)
items.abstract: Audio-visual target speaker extraction (AV-TSE) leverages visual information to recover a target speech signal from multi-speaker mixtures. However, existing systems are often built with non-causal architectures and incur high computational cost, which limits real-time deployment. While some studies reduce the overall complexity by designing lighter separation backbones, comparatively little attention has been paid to improving deployability by optimizing the visual branch. In this work, we revisit the design of visual cues and employ visemes as the visual guidance signal. Compared with conventional VSR-pretrained visual representations, viseme pretraining yields a more lightweight, robust, and interpretable cue. In addition, we propose an online viseme-guided TSE system that achieves strong performance under the lowest computational budget.

items.title: LLM-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Audio-Visual Speech Enhancement
items.authors: Chih-Ning Chen(National Taiwan University); Jen-Cheng Hou(Academia Sinica); Hsin-Min Wang(Academia Sinica); Shao-Yi Chien(National Taiwan University); Yu Tsao(Academia Sinica); Fan-Gang Zeng(University of California Irvine)
items.abstract: In existing Audio-Visual Speech Enhancement (AVSE) methods, objectives such as Scale-Invariant Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SI-SNR) and Mean Squared Error (MSE) are widely used; however, their correlation with perceived speech quality is often suboptimal and provides limited interpretability for optimization. This work proposes a reinforcement learning-based AVSE framework with a Large Language Model (LLM)-based interpretable reward model. An audio LLM generates natural language descriptions of enhanced speech, which are converted by a sentiment analysis model into a 1-5 rating score serving as the PPO reward for fine-tuning a pretrained AVSE model. Compared with scalar metrics, LLM-generated feedback is semantically rich and explicitly describes speech quality improvements. Experiments on the AVSEC-4 dataset show that the proposed method outperforms a supervised baseline and a DNSMOS-based RL baseline in PESQ, STOI, neural quality metrics, and subjective listening tests.

items.title: MOS-Bias: From Hidden Gender Bias to Gender-Aware Speech Quality Assessment
items.authors: Wenze Ren(National Taiwan University); Yi-Cheng Lin(National Taiwan University); Wen-Chin Huang(Nagoya University); Erica Cooper(National Institute of Information and Communications Technology); Ryandhimas Zezario(Academia Sinica); Hsin-Min Wang(Academia Sinica); Hung-yi Lee(National Taiwan University); Yu Tsao(Academia Sinica)
items.abstract: The Mean Opinion Score (MOS) serves as the standard metric for speech quality assessment, yet biases in human annotations remain underexplored. We conduct the first systematic analysis of gender bias in MOS, revealing that male listeners consistently assign higher scores than female listeners, a gap that is most pronounced in low-quality speech and gradually diminishes as quality improves. This quality-dependent structure proves difficult to eliminate through simple calibration. We further demonstrate that automated MOS models trained on aggregated labels exhibit predictions skewed toward male standards of perception. To address this, we propose a gender-aware model that learns gender-specific scoring patterns through abstract binary group embeddings, thereby improving overall and gender-specific prediction accuracy. This study establishes that gender bias in MOS constitutes a systematic, learnable pattern demanding attention in equitable speech evaluation.

items.title: TDScore: Learning Synthetic Speech Quality Predictors from TTS Training Dynamics without Human annotation
items.authors: Natacha Miniconi(Le Mans Université); Meysam Shamsi(Le Mans Université); Anthony Larcher(Le Mans Université)
items.abstract: Subjective listening tests are the standard for evaluating synthetic speech quality, but they are costly, time-consuming, and difficult to scale. Automatic speech synthetic quality predictors reduce reliance on human ratings, but still depend on large amounts of human-annotated data and generalize poorly across languages, speakers, and synthesis paradigms. This paper proposes a framework without human annotation for learning synthetic speech quality predictors by exploiting training dynamics of text-to-speech systems as pseudo annotation. Synthetic speech is collected from multiple TTS models at different training checkpoints and paired with training-derived metadata such as iteration index and loss. A quality predictor is trained from audio without human perceptual labels. Experiments on benchmark datasets covering multiple languages show that iteration annotation correlates with human annotation across datasets and languages.

items.title: Exploring Active Sampling Strategies for Pairwise Comparisons in Speech Synthesis Evaluation
items.authors: Cassia Valentini-Botinhao(The University of Edinburgh); Andrea Lorena Aldana Blanco(The University of Edinburgh); Dan Wells(The University of Edinburgh); Aidan Pine(National Research Council Canada); Korin Richmond(The University of Edinburgh)
items.abstract: Subjective tests are the gold standard for text-to-speech evaluation. Tests based on preference tasks are favoured by participants and are less prone to listener-dependent biases. Despite their advantages, preference-based tests are less widely adopted than absolute rating tests like MOS due to the misconception that all possible pairs must be tested in order for results to be reliable. In this paper, we compare different approaches for pair selection in AB and BWS tests, contrasting random selection with two active sampling methods: a sorting-based method and an information-gain-based method called ASAP. We found that the ASAP method reveals more significant differences compared to others, and that BWS tests are more effective than AB tests for the same test duration. This is evident in both number of significant differences and system rank correlation, with ASAP further amplifying the improvements.

items.title: Decoding the Ear (DeEAR): A Framework for Objectifying Expressiveness from Human Preference Through Efficient Alignment
items.authors: Zhiyu Lin(The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen; Li Auto Inc.); Jingwen Yang(The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen; Li Auto Inc.); Jiale Zhao(Li Auto Inc.); Meng Liu(Li Auto Inc.); Sunzhu Li(Li Auto Inc.); Zhengjun Yue(The Chinese University of Hong Kong; Shenzhen Loop Area Institution); Benyou Wang(The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen; Shenzhen Loop Area Institution)
items.abstract: Recent speech-to-speech (S2S) models generate intelligible speech but often lack natural expressiveness. A key bottleneck is the absence of an objective, automatic metric of expressiveness. Existing approaches rely on subjective ratings or low-level acoustic features, which are either costly and unscalable or fail to capture perceptual nuance. We introduce DeEAR, a framework that maps human perception of expressiveness to objective scores. Grounded in phonetics and psychology, DeEAR evaluates speech along three dimensions: Emotion, Prosody, and Spontaneity. With fewer than 500 annotated samples, it achieves strong agreement with expert ratings (SRCC=0.85). DeEAR further enables scalable benchmarking and evaluation-driven data curation. Using DeEAR, we curate 14K expressive utterances to build a bilingual ExpressiveSpeech dataset and fine-tune an S2S model, leading to clear improvements in perceived expressiveness in human evaluations.

items.title: CodecMOS-Accent: A MOS Benchmark of Resynthesized and TTS Speech from Neural Codecs Across English Accents
items.authors: Wen-Chin Huang(Nagoya University); Nicholas Sanders(University of Edinburgh); Erica Cooper(National Institute Of Information And Communications Technology)
items.abstract: We present the CodecMOS-Accent dataset, a mean opinion score (MOS) benchmark designed to evaluate neural audio codec (NAC) models and the large language model (LLM)-based text-to-speech (TTS) models trained upon them, especially across non-standard speech like accented speech. The dataset comprises 4,000 codec resynthesis and TTS samples from 24 systems, featuring 32 speakers spanning ten accents. A large-scale subjective test was conducted to collect 19,600 annotations from 25 listeners across three dimensions: naturalness, speaker similarity, and accent similarity. This dataset does not only represent an up-to-date study of recent speech synthesis system performance but reveals insights including a tight relationship between speaker and accent similarity, the predictive power of objective metrics, and a perceptual bias when listeners share the same accent with the speaker. This dataset is expected to foster research on more human-centric evaluation for NAC and accented TTS.

items.title: MMGenre: Benchmarking Singing Voice Synthesis across Multiple Musical Genres
items.authors: Wenhao Feng(Renmin University of China); Yuxun Tang(Renmin University of China); Jiatong Shi(Carnegie Mellon University); Qin Jin(Renmin University of China)
items.abstract: Singing voice synthesis (SVS) has progressed rapidly, yet its ability to generalize across diverse musical genres remains underexplored. Existing benchmarks are heavily biased toward pop music, limiting systematic analysis of genre-dependent behavior. We introduce MMGenre, a benchmark for multi-genre SVS diagnosis, supported by an automatic pipeline for constructing genre-aligned music scores. MMGenre spans 10 major genres and 26 subgenres, enabling comprehensive analysis of genre-aware synthesis. Extensive evaluation of representative SVS models reveals limited genre discrimination: synthesized vocals across genres exhibit highly similar acoustic characteristics and weak separability. While zero-shot genre adaptation yields only marginal improvements, lightweight genre-specific continued training leads to substantial gains. MMGenre provides a standardized framework for multi-genre SVS evaluation and exposes critical challenges in achieving genre-aware singing voice synthesis.

items.title: Rubric-Aligned Disentangled Evaluation of Human Simultaneous Interpreting
items.authors: Ziyu Zhang(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Satoshi Nakamura(The Chinese University of Hong Kong; Shenzhen Loop Area Institute,)
items.abstract: Human simultaneous interpreting (SI) is commonly assessed with analytic rubrics separating meaning transfer, delivery quality, and temporal synchrony, yet no automatic metric is designed for rubric-aligned segment-level SI evaluation. We construct a professionally annotated corpus of 1,101 SI segments with scores for meaning transfer (LQ), delivery quality (EXP), and perceived latency (LAT). We show that structured LLM prompting and scalar supervision collapse rubric dimensions, yielding near-zero correlation with human ratings and strong cross-dimension coupling. To isolate supervision structure under identical backbone capacity, we introduce dual regression heads on a LoRA-adapted COMET-KIWI encoder. On a held-out talk-level test set, the model achieves Pearson correlations of 0.388 (LQ) and 0.301 (EXP), improving over frozen COMET-KIWI. Given low absolute rater agreement, we interpret results relative to human consistency and target stable ranking signals for formative assessment.

items.title: ARTIST: Universal Articulatory Space Modeling for Multilingual Indic-to-English Speech-to-Speech Translation
items.authors: Khushal Yadav(IIIT-Delhi); Vinayak Abrol(IIIT-Delhi)
items.abstract: We present ARTIST, a novel end-to-end framework for multilingual Indic-to-English Speech-to-Speech Translation (S2ST) operating in a universal articulatory space. It utilizes a Conformer encoder with intermediate CTC supervision over source articulatory features, explicitly aligning diverse acoustic inputs with quantized, language-agnostic representations. To map these features, we introduce a Convolution-Augmented Differential Transformer decoder designed to capture both local phonetic nuances and global context. We demonstrate exceptional cross-lingual transfer across 11 Indic languages, including extreme low-resource settings (10hr/language). For instance, with only 166M parameters, ARTIST outperforms the 1.2B parameter SeamlessM4T baseline on BLEU, COMET, and chrF. ARTIST also achieves superior VRAM efficiency, establishing a high-performance paradigm for scaling direct S2ST to resource-constrained environments.

items.title: Evaluating and Preserving Lexical Stress in English-to-Chinese Speech-to-Speech Translation
items.authors: Yuchen Song(The Chinese University of Hong Kong-Shenzhen; Shenzhen Loop Area Institute); Xi Chen(The Chinese University of Hong Kong-Shenzhen); Mingze Li(The Chinese University of Hong Kong-Shenzhen); Satoshi Nakamura(The Chinese University of Hong Kong-Shenzhen)
items.abstract: Speech-to-speech translation (S2ST) systems have achieved impressive progress in semantic accuracy and speech naturalness. However, the cross-lingual transfer of lexical stress-a vital cue for emphasis and speaker intent-remains heavily under-explored, compounded by a lack of reliable automatic evaluation metrics for tonal languages like Chinese. We investigate English-to-Chinese S2ST stress transfer by constructing a stress-annotated Chinese dataset and an XLS-R-based Mandarin stress detector. Integrating this with the English EmphAssess system, we propose a novel objective metric for cross-lingual stress evaluation. Furthermore, we fine-tune CosyVoice3 to build a stress-aware S2ST system. Experiments demonstrate that our proposed S2ST architecture significantly outperforms existing systems in stress translation capability while maintaining competitive translation quality. Furthermore, our evaluation metric exhibits a strong correlation with human subjective judgments.

items.title: Listening or Reading? Evaluating Speech Awareness in Chain-of-Thought Speech-to-Text Translation
items.authors: Jacobo Romero-Díaz(BSC); Gerard I. Gállego(BSC; UPC); Oriol Pareras(BSC); Federico Costa(BSC; UPC); Javier Hernando(BSC; UPC); Cristina España-Bonet(BSC; DFKI GmbH)
items.abstract: Speech-to-Text Translation (S2TT) systems that cascade Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-to-Text Translation (T2TT) are fundamentally limited by error propagation and the loss of prosodic cues. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting was introduced to address these limitations by providing joint access to both speech and transcription during generation. In this study, we systematically evaluate CoT's actual speech awareness through input attribution analysis, assessment of robustness against corrupted transcripts, and prosody-awareness evaluation. Our results indicate that CoT largely replicates cascaded behavior, relying heavily on textual transcripts. By applying simple training interventions (e.g., injecting noisy transcripts in the CoT), we demonstrate enhanced model robustness and increased acoustic reliance. Our findings challenge the presumed benefits of CoT S2TT and emphasize the necessity for techniques that help integrate acoustic information into the translation process.

items.title: A Multimodal Semi-Supervised Framework for Automatic Construction of a Cross-Lingual Taigi Speech-Chinese Subtitle Corpus
items.authors: Cheng-Hsiu Cho(National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University); Chih-Chung Kuo(National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University); Yu-Siang Lan(National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University); Chao-Shih Huang(National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University); Yan-Ming Lin(National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University); Yuan-Fu Liao(National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University)
items.abstract: The lack of labeled data for low-resource languages such as Taigi (Taiwanese) limits AI development. This work addresses the issue by exploiting online videos containing Taigi speech with hard-coded Chinese subtitles. We propose a multimodal semi-supervised framework that combines a trimodal Audio-Visual-Language Model (AVLM) with an iterative pseudo-labeling process inspired by knowledge distillation. A Vision-Language Model fuses OCR outputs and AVLM predictions to generate refined subtitles, enabling automatic construction of a large-scale Taigi speech-Chinese subtitle corpus from unlabeled videos. Experiments show that the AVLM reduces subtitle recognition CER from 36.8% to 9.3%. The resulting 860-hour corpus improves downstream tasks: Whisper's cross-lingual transcription CER decreases from 57.8% to 37.8%, and Taigi-Chinese translation BLEU doubles from 0.2016 to 0.4033. These results demonstrate an effective and transferable paradigm for low-resource corpus construction.

items.title: AfriVox-v2: A Domain-Verticalized Benchmark for In-the-Wild African Speech Recognition
items.authors: Busayo Awobade(Intron ); Gabrial Ashungafac(Intron ); Oluwatoni Otokiti(Intron ); Tobi Olatunji(Intron )
items.abstract: Recent large language models (LLMs) show strong speech recognition and translation capabilities for high-resource languages. However, African languages remain dramatically underrepresented in benchmarks, limiting their practical use in low-resource settings. While early benchmarks tested African languages and accents, they lacked exhaustive real-world noise and granular domain evaluations. We present AfriVox-v2, a comprehensive benchmark designed to test speech models under realistic African deployment conditions. AfriVox-v2 introduces "in the wild" unscripted audio for all supported languages. We also introduce strict domain verticalization, evaluating model accuracy across ten sectors including government, finance, health, and agriculture and conducting targeted tests on numbers and named entities. Finally, we benchmark a new generation of speech models, including Sahara-v2, Gemini 3 Flash, and the Omnilingual CTC models. Our results expose the true generalization gap of modern speech models in specialized, noisy African contexts and provide a reliable blueprint for developers building localized voice AI.

items.title: Correct Then Detect: Zero-Shot FVMC Annotation for Child Language Sample Analysis
items.authors: Shuwei Hou(University at Buffalo); Wei Bo(University at Buffalo); Varun Shijo(University at Buffalo); Chuhui Liu(University at Buffalo); Manav Kanaganapalli(University at Buffalo); Ling-Yu Guo(University at Buffalo); Wenyao Xu(University at Buffalo)
items.abstract: The Finite Verb Morphology Composite (FVMC) is a clinically validated metric for identifying Developmental Language Disorder (DLD), yet its computation requires labor-intensive manual annotation of obligatory tense contexts. Since no annotated corpora exist for training, large language models (LLMs) have been the only approach to automated FVMC annotation. Rather than prompting LLMs end-to-end, we present the first zero-shot framework that decomposes the task into grammar correction and obligatory context detection, followed by alignment to label each context as correct, incorrect, or omitted. Evaluated on the ENNI child narrative dataset, our best configurations achieve F1 scores of 97.05%, 60.15%, and 70.23% for correct, incorrect, and omitted contexts, improving by 1.99, 4.72, and 6.21 points over the strongest LLMs as of February 2026 (GPT 5.2 and Sonnet 4.6 Reasoning Models). The proposed paradigm enables scalable, cost-efficient automated language assessment.

items.title: Detection of Incorrect Place of Articulation in Polish Sibilants Using Convolutional Autoencoders
items.authors: Wojciech Pieniążek(Silesian University of Technology); Oliwia Skórzewska(Silesian University of Technology); Maria Filipek(Silesian University of Technology); Zuzanna Miodońska(Silesian University of Technology)
items.abstract: Incorrect production of sibilant consonants is among the most common speech disorders in children, and its effective treatment depends on early diagnosis. This study proposes and investigates a method for detecting the incorrect place of articulation in productions of Polish voiceless retroflex fricatives and affricates in child speech. The approach combines convolutional autoencoders (classical, sparse, and multi-task variants) for feature extraction with support vector machines. The speech corpus included children aged 4-8 years: 149 speakers for fricative and 151 for affricate sounds. The best-performing models employ multi-task learning achieving sensitivities of up to 84.32%. The results demonstrate that autoencoder-based embeddings are effective for feature extraction and classification in challenging pediatric speech datasets.

items.title: SpiroPhonia: Non-Invasive Respiratory Health Assessment from Spontaneous Speech
items.authors: Roksana Khanom(University of Maryland); Shafia Supty(DR. M R Khan Shishu Hospital & Institute of Child Health); Nirupam Roy(University of Maryland); Ashok Agrawala(University of Maryland)
items.abstract: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) remains a major global health challenge, emphasizing the need for accessible and non-invasive detection. Since speech production is fundamentally linked to respiratory physiology, its disruptions can serve as indirect indicators of pulmonary impairment. This study introduces SpiroPhonia, a machine learning framework that leverages spontaneous speech for respiratory health assessment. We evaluated SpiroPhonia on a new dataset of 201 speakers (102 with COPD, 99 healthy controls). By integrating statistical analysis with recursive feature selection, we identified a compact set of discriminative speech markers. Our best model achieved 78% accuracy, 80% F1-score, and 87% AUC. This performance on spontaneous speech is competitive with methods using controlled laboratory recordings. Findings demonstrate that everyday speech encodes robust respiratory biomarkers, paving the way for continuous health monitoring via voice-enabled technologies.

items.title: Effects of Co-speech Gesture on the Acoustic Realization of Focus in Cantonese-speaking Children With and Without Autism Spectrum Disorder
items.authors: Zhuoran Li(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Si Chen(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Yitian Hong(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Bingxin Liu(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Ho-Yi Ku(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Jiayue Gao(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Chun-Sing Wong(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Angel Chan(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Zhuoming Chen(The First Affiliated Hospital of Jinan University); Haoyan Ge(Hong Kong Metropolitan University); Bin Li(City University of Hong Kong); Li Sheng(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Po-yi Tempo Tang(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Ratree Wayland(University of Florida)
items.abstract: The effect of co-speech gesture on the acoustic realization of focus remains comparatively understudied. Children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) show diﬀiculties in both prosodic focus marking and gesture-speech integration. This study investigated how co-speech gesture shapes focus prosody in 22 autistic and 25 typically developing (TD) Cantonese-speaking children. The results indicated that iconic gestures increased the duration of on-target syllables in both groups. However, TD children shortened the duration of post-focus syllables across gesture types, reinforcing the prosodic prominence of the on-focus syllable. In contrast, the ASD group exhibited distinct patterns: a duration-shortening effect was observed for both on-target and post-target syllables with deictic gestures. The results are in line with the Weak Central Coherence theory and the Enhanced Perceptual Functioning Model of ASD, which posit diﬀiculties with multimodal integration.

items.title: Paediatric-HGNN: A Hybrid Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network for Detecting Disfluency in Children’s Speech via Multiscale Acoustic Fusion
items.authors: Rashini Liyanarachchi(University of New South Wales); Rachael Mackay(Resourced Music Therapy); Alison Short(Western Sydney University); Aditya Joshi(University of New South Wales); Erik Meijering(University of New South Wales)
items.abstract: Automated stuttering detection (ASD) systems struggle with paediatric speech due to high acoustic variability in developing voices and the subtle distinction between pathological stuttering and typical developmental disfluencies. We introduce Paediatric-HGNN, a framework using a Сontext-aware Part-whole Interaction Network (CaPIN) tailored for paediatric data. Instead of conventional 1D signal modelling, our approach builds a heterogeneous graph capturing hierarchical relationships between lexical units (word nodes) and fine-grained acoustic segments (frame nodes). Trained on curated paediatric corpora (UCLASS and FluencyBank), Paediatric-HGNN achieves 82.4% weighted accuracy and a Typical Disfluency F1-score of 0.386. Modelling hierarchical lexical-acoustic interactions captures developmental "searching" behaviour, offering a more robust and interpretable tool for early clinical intervention.

items.title: Reasoning Beyond Transcription: Audio Language Models on Child Stuttering Speech
items.authors: Chibuzor Okocha(University of Florida); Christan Grant(University of Florida); Zoey Liu(University of Florida)
items.abstract: Child speech differs from adult speech in acoustics, prosody, and linguistic structures. Speech disfluencies (such as repetitions) further challenge automatic understanding. While Audio–Language Models (ALMs) show strong semantic reasoning from speech audio, their ability to reason about disfluent child speech in mixed-speaker settings remains unexplored. We investigate this through two tasks: child-focused semantic summarization and speech entailment. Experiments use recordings of children who stutter in mixed-speaker interviews without explicit speaker separation. Models are instruction-guided to focus on the child, preserve clinically relevant disfluencies, and avoid adult-speech leakage. Evaluation combines LLM-based judges and reference-based metrics, anchored by transcript-oracle baselines to isolate errors. Results show that while ALMs extract high-level meaning from stuttered speech, reasoning degrades significantly with increased disfluency and speaker interference.
