items.title: Unlocking In-Context Learning in Audio-Language Models from Decentralized Medical Audio
items.authors: Ran Piao(Eindhoven University of Technology); Tsai-Ning Wang(Eindhoven University of Technology); Martijn den Dekker(Erasmus MC); Linda Moonen(Rijnstate Hospital); Hareld Kemps(Máxima MC Hospital); Yuan Lu(Eindhoven University of Technology); Aaqib Saeed(Eindhoven University of Technology)
items.abstract: Clinical audio diagnosis in low-resource settings requires models that identify conditions from minimal examples without large annotated corpora. We propose Federated Self-Contextualization (FSC), a multimodal language model framework for in-context clinical audio diagnosis across federated hospital clients. FSC constructs pseudo-label episodes via unsupervised clustering of audio representations, bypassing scarce real diagnostic labels, and enables contextual reasoning from support-query pairs. Our progressive three-stage pipeline first aligns audio embeddings with the language model via caption-based pretraining, then adapts it for episodic in-context inference through federated optimization. At test time, given a small labeled support set, the model diagnoses an unseen query through multimodal reasoning. On held-out respiratory and cardiac conditions, FSC achieves 71.6% accuracy in 2-way 2-shot evaluation, outperforming audio-language baselines by over 9%.

items.title: Speech-based Psychological Crisis Assessment using LLMs
items.authors: Terumi Chiba(Tsinghua University); Yang Luo(Peking University Huilongguan Clinical Medical School, Beijing; WHO Collaborating Centre for Research and Training in Suicide Prevention); Ziyun Cui(Tsinghua University); Yongsheng Tong(Peking University Huilongguan Clinical Medical School; WHO Collaborating Centre for Research and Training in Suicide Prevention); Chao Zhang(Tsinghua University)
items.abstract: Psychological support hotlines provide critical support for individuals experiencing mental health emergencies, yet crisis-level assessment largely relies on human operators whose judgments may vary with training and staffing constraints. This paper studies automated three-way crisis-level classification from authentic hotline speech under privacy-sensitive and data-scarce conditions. We propose an LLM-based pipeline that converts non-verbal acoustic cues into explicit textual evidence through paralinguistic injection, enabling a text LLM to use vocal affect that is otherwise lost in ASR transcripts. We also explore reasoning-enhanced training, where LLM-generated diagnostic rationales are used as auxiliary supervision to regularise the classification objective. With chunk-based data augmentation and 5-fold cross-validation, our system achieves a macro F1-score of 0.802 and an accuracy of 0.805, outperforming acoustic, zero-shot LLM, and speech-aware LLM baselines.

items.title: Investigating LLMs Behavior in Depression Severity Prediction
items.authors: Jiawei Yu(Utrecht University); Yun Hao(University of Groningen); Heysem Kaya(Utrecht University)
items.abstract: Large language models are increasingly applied to depression assessment, yet it remains unclear whether few-shot learning provides effective supervision for depression severity prediction. We conduct a study on PHQ-8 prediction, evaluating five LLMs across 0-10-shot settings and introducing a contradictory-label intervention to test label dependence. Across models, increasing shot count yields limited and non-monotonic gains, and performance is largely insensitive to corrupted demonstration labels, suggesting that few-shot examples may serve more as structural cues than effective supervision. In contrast, replacing full transcripts with symptom-focused excerpts consistently improves performance while reducing token usage by approximately 80% per session. Prediction averaging further provides stable gains without modifying prompt design. Our findings indicate that context relevance matters more than demonstration quantity, offering guidance for cost-effective clinical deployment.

items.title: Beyond WER: A Paired Acoustic Stress Test for Ambient Clinical Scribes
items.authors: Xiao-Hang Jiang(USTC); Han-Jie Guo(USTC); Ying-Si Liang(USTC); Yang Ai(USTC); Zhen-Hua Ling(USTC); Lei Jiang(iFLYTEK); Zhi-Yang He(iFLYTEK)
items.abstract: Ambient clinical scribes increasingly combine Automatic Speech Recognition with Large Language Models to automate documentation. However, traditional metrics like Word Error Rate mask systemic safety degradation. We present a paired acoustic stress test to isolate the causal impact of noise on clinical reasoning. For the same dialogues, we inject diverse noise types while keeping the downstream model configuration frozen. Crucially, we uncover a dangerous disconnect between signal fidelity and clinical safety. Stationary ambient noise increased the Word Error Rate by a negligible 0.71 percentage points yet nearly doubled the rate of unsafe outputs. Our analysis reveals that minor acoustic perturbations can invert clinical meaning without substantially inflating error rates. Furthermore, we demonstrate a lightweight mitigation strategy that mitigates safety degradation under noisy conditions without requiring model fine tuning.

items.title: Benchmarking Speech Systems for Frontline Health Conversations: The DISPLACE-M Challenge
items.authors: Dhanya E(IISc); Ankita Meena(IISc); Manas Nanivadekar(IISc); Noumida A(Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore); Victor Azad(Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore); Ashwini Nagaraj Shenoy(NITK); Pratik Roy Chowdhuri(NITK); Shobhit Banga(Josh Talks); Vanshika Chhabra(Josh Talks); Chitralekha Bhati(IISc); Shareef babu Kalluri(MAHE); Srikanth Raj Chetupalli(IIT Bombay); Deepu Vijayasenan(NITK); Sriram Ganapathy(IISc)
items.abstract: The DIarization and Speech Processing for LAnguage understanding in Conversational Environments - Medical (DISPLACE-M) challenge introduces a conversational AI benchmark for understanding goal-oriented, real-world medical dialogues. The challenge addresses multi-speaker interactions between frontline health workers and care seekers, characterized by spontaneous, noisy and overlapping speech. As part of the challenge, medical conversational dataset comprising 40 hours of development and 15 hours of blind evaluation recordings was released. We provided baseline systems across 4 tasks - speaker diarization, automatic speech recognition, topic identification and dialogue summarization - to enable consistent benchmarking. System performance is evaluated using diarization error rate (DER), time-constrained minimum-permutation word error rate (tcpWER) and ROUGE-L. This paper describes the Phase-I evaluation - data, tasks and baseline systems - along with the summary of the evaluation results.

items.title: AuscuTSLM: Patient-Level Multimodal Question Answering from Multi-Site Auscultation Recordings
items.authors: Fan Wu(ETH Zurich); Tsai-Ning Wang(Eindhoven University of Technology); Nicolas Zumarraga(ETH Zurich); Ning Wang(ETH Zurich); Markus Kreft(ETH Zurich); Kevin O'Sullivan(ETH Zurich); Paula Manso Zorrilla(); Elgar Fleisch(ETH Zurich; University of St. Gallen); Oliver Aalami(Stanford University); Paul Schmiedmayer(Stanford University); Robert Jakob(ETH Zurich); Patrick Langer(ETH Zurich; Stanford University)
items.abstract: Auscultation is a vital diagnostic tool, yet its utility is often limited by subjective interpretation. While general-purpose Audio-Language Models (ALMs) excel in general domains, they struggle with the nuances of physiological signals. We propose a framework that aligns multi-site auscultation recordings directly with a frozen Large Language Model (LLM) embedding space via gated cross-attention. By leveraging the LLM's latent world knowledge, our approach moves beyond isolated classification toward holistic, patient-level assessment. On the CaReSound benchmark, our model achieves a state-of-the-art 0.865 F1-macro and 0.952 BERTScore. We demonstrate that lightweight, domain-specific encoders rival large-scale ALMs and that multi-site aggregation provides spatial redundancy that mitigates temporal truncation. This alignment of medical acoustics with text foundations offers a scalable path for bridging signal processing and clinical assessment.

items.title: WASIL: In-the-Wild Arabic Spoken Interactions with LLMs
items.authors: Zien Sheikh Ali(Qatar Computing Research Institute); Hamdy Mubarak(Qatar Computing Research Institute); Soon-Gyo Jung(Qatar Computing Research Institute); Hunzalah Hassan Bhatti(Qatar Computing Research Institute); Firoj Alam(Qatar Computing Research Institute); Shammur Absar Chowdhury(Qatar Computing Research Institute)
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) voice assistants are commonly built as cascaded Automatic Speech recognition (ASR) → LLM systems, where recognition errors can distort user intent. Dislikes may also arise from ambiguous, out-of-domain, or non-request turns, making it hard to isolate ASR effects. We release WASIL, in-the-wild Arabic spoken interaction prompts with audio, ASR hypotheses, assistant responses, and explicit like/dislike feedback, covering Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) and four major dialects with their labels. We provide low-cost gold transcripts via multi-ASR agreement-guided post-editing and annotate answerability (answerable, ambiguous/needs-clarification, unsupported, not-a-request/noise) to separate intrinsic unanswerability from ASR-induced degradation. Finally, we describe scalable reference-free evaluation of responses from ASR vs. gold transcripts using multi-judge LLM scoring.

items.title: When Machines Speak Like Local Peers: Improving Conversational Experiences with Accent-Adaptive Voice Agents
items.authors: Shubhangi S. R. Garnaik(The State University of New York; Stony Brook University); JiHyun Jeong(The State University of New York; Stony Brook University); Jihoon Ryoo(The State University of New York; Stony Brook University)
items.abstract: Public voice agents often underperform for accented English, reducing usability and trust. LocalMATE is an end-to-end accent-adaptive airport conversational agent that (i) estimates a user's accent with calibrated confidence, (ii) retrieves grounded answers, and (iii) returns accent-conditioned speech with a synchronized talking-face video, using a confidence-gated fallback when uncertain. Our accent estimator (WavLM-Base-Plus with layer-weighted statistics pooling) reaches 85% speaker-disjoint accuracy on L2-ARCTIC (Indian/Korean/Spanish) and 92.3% on out-of-domain Korean-accented Speech Accent Archive. items.title: Evaluating Large Language Models Abilities for Addressee, Turn-change, and Next Speaker Prediction in Meetings
items.authors: Ryo Fukuda(NTT); Takatomo Kano(NTT); Siddhant Arora(Carnegie Mellon University); Marc Delcroix(NTT); Naohiro Tawara(NTT); Atsunori Ogawa(NTT); Yuya Chiba(NTT); Atsushi Ando(NTT); William Chen(Carnegie Mellon University); Shinji Watanabe(Carnegie Mellon University)
items.abstract: We investigate turn-taking in multimodal multi-party conversations using large language models (LLMs). We construct an evaluation framework for three tasks: addressee detection, turn-change prediction, and next speaker prediction. We compare supervised models trained for these tasks, text-based LLMs, multimodal LLMs (MM-LLMs), and human subjects. Experiments on the AMI corpus showed that LLMs outperformed supervised models and humans in next speaker prediction, despite not being trained on the target domain and without access to audio or visual information. An MM-LLM performed better than text-based LLMs on addressee detection and turn-change prediction but remained below human performance, indicating difficulty leveraging raw audio-visual signals. Ablation analyses revealed that conversational context was critical, particularly for next speaker prediction. We observed that human and LLM prediction patterns were similar, and intervals with frequent turn changes were difficult for both.

items.title: MuVAP: Multimodal Multiparty Voice Activity Projection for Turn-taking Prediction in the wild
items.authors: Haotian Qi(KTH); Gabriel Skantze(KTH)
items.abstract: Current multiparty turn-taking models often rely on complex microphone arrays or multi-camera setups, limiting their applicability in human-robot interaction scenarios. We introduce MuVAP, a causal multimodal framework that extends Voice Activity Projection by grounding acoustic predictions in face tracks, enabling speaker-aware turn-taking predictions from a monaural audio stream and a single camera view. To address the combinatorial complexity of modeling multiple speakers, we propose Role-Relative Projection, which maps any N-speaker interaction onto a fixed current versus next floor-holder state. Because existing audiovisual datasets contain disruptive editing cuts that break causal tracking, we introduce the Audio-Visual Conversation Corpus, a 31-hour dataset of unedited, single-camera multiparty conversations. Evaluations demonstrate that MuVAP outperforms strong baselines on Shift-Hold and next-speaker prediction tasks across two-and three-speaker settings.

items.title: TurnGuide: Enhancing Meaningful Full Duplex Spoken Interactions via Dynamic Turn-Level Text-Speech Interleaving
items.authors: Wenqian Cui(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Lei Zhu(Huawei Technologies); Xiao-Hui Li(Huawei Technologies); Zhihan Guo(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Haoli Bai(Huawei Technologies); Lu Hou(Huawei Technologies); Irwin King(The Chinese University of Hong Kong)
items.abstract: Full-Duplex Speech Language Models (FD-SLMs) enable real-time spoken interaction by modeling turn-taking behaviors such as interruptions and overlapping speech. End-to-end (e2e) FD-SLMs learn from double-channel conversational audio to capture natural dialogue dynamics, but their conversational quality often degrades compared to text-only models due to long speech sequences and limited high-quality spoken data. Although interleaved text-speech generation may alleviate this issue, inserting discrete text tokens into continuous dual-channel audio can disrupt temporal alignment and interaction fluency. We propose TurnGuide, a turn-level text-speech interleaved framework that dynamically segments assistant speech and jointly generates text and speech. This enables semantic intelligence from LLMs while preserving natural acoustic flow. Experiments show that TurnGuide significantly improves semantic coherence and achieves state-of-the-art performance on diverse turn-taking events.

items.title: Revisiting Active Speaker Detection: An In-the-Wild Benchmark for Generalization and Robustness
items.authors: Le Thien Phuc Nguyen(University of Wisconsin - Madison); Zhuoran Yu(University of Wisconsin - Madison); Khoa Quang Nhat Cao(University of Wisconsin - Madison); Yuwei Guo(University of Wisconsin - Madison); Tu Ho Manh Pham(University of Wisconsin - Madison); Tuan Tai Nguyen(University of Wisconsin - Madison); Toan Ngo Duc Vo(University of Wisconsin - Madison); Lucas Poon(Oregon State University); Tuan Khai Nguyen(University of Sydney); Soochahn Lee(Kookmin University); Yong Jae Lee(University of Wisconsin - Madison)
items.abstract: We present UniTalk, a novel dataset emphasizing challenging scenarios to enhance model generalization for the task of active speaker detection (ASD). Previously established benchmarks such as AVA predominantly comprise old movies and thus exhibit significant domain gaps with real-world video. In contrast, UniTalk covers diverse video types reflecting challenging real-world conditions, including underrepresented languages, noisy backgrounds, and crowded scenes, while being on par with AVA in scale. Extensive evaluations reveal that ASD remains unsolved under realistic conditions: state-of-the-art models near-perfect on AVA fail to reach saturation on UniTalk. Conversely, models trained on UniTalk generalize better to modern in-the-wild datasets including Talkies and ASW. UniTalk thus establishes a new benchmark for ASD, providing researchers with a valuable resource for developing and evaluating versatile and resilient models.

items.title: ECAPA-TDNN-based Speaker Embedding Framework for Voice Mimicry Assessment
items.authors: Bhasi K.C.(Government Engineering College Barton Hill; APJ Abdul Kalam Technological University); Rajeev Rajan(Government Engineering College Idukki; APJ Abdul Kalam Technological University)
items.abstract: This paper investigates the quality of impersonated (mimicked) speech by extracting speaker embeddings from both spectral and prosodic features. Prosodic features analyzed include loudness, pitch, speaking rate, shimmer, and tempogram ratio, while spectral features cover MFCCs (Mel Frequency Cepstral Coefficeints), chroma, tonnetz, spectral roll-off, spectral bandwidth, spectral flux, and spectral centroid. The evaluation begins with a perception test to identify the best mimicked artist. The study then explores whether a Deep Neural Network (DNN) can predict this artist based on the Mean Opinion Score (MOS) test. A correct prediction, called a "hit", occurs when the model's output matches the top-rated artist. Model performance is measured using a top-1 ranking on the MIMICz dataset. Results show that augmented speaker embeddings derived from Emphasized Channel Attention, Propagation and Aggregation (ECAPA) embeddings outperform those derived from other embedding methods.

items.title: Do speech representational spaces encode language family structures?
items.authors: Emily Gaughan(The University of Edinburgh); Peter Bell(The University of Edinburgh)
items.abstract: Learned speech representations are known to contain information about the language spoken, but to what extent do they encode meaningful language family structure? We believe that answering this question is important if we are to incorporate knowledge of language relationships and change into future speech models, to better represent low resource languages and non-standard variants. In this paper, we compare approaches to measuring language family structure in representational spaces, when encapsulated in the form of phylogenetic trees. We analyse six existing tree comparison methods, demonstrating their complementary nature, and show that tree-based methods account for more language family structure than probing classifiers. We evaluate the representation spaces of six common speech encoders or LID models, comparing to a linguistic lexicostatistical top line, and find interesting differences between seen representations, particularly with respect to languages not seen during training.

items.title: Quantifying Dimensional Independence in Speech: An Information-Theoretic Framework for Disentangled Representation Learning
items.authors: Bipasha Kashyap(Deakin University); Björn W. Schuller(TUM University Hospital; Imperial College London); Pubudu N. Pathirana(Deakin University)
items.abstract: Speech signals encode emotional, linguistic, and pathological information within a shared acoustic channel; however, disentanglement is typically assessed indirectly through downstream task performance. We introduce an information-theoretic framework to quantify cross-dimension statistical dependence in handcrafted acoustic features by integrating bounded neural mutual information (MI) estimation with non-parametric validation. Across six corpora, cross-dimension MI remains low, with tight estimation bounds (< 0.15 nats), indicating weak statistical coupling in the data considered, whereas Source-Filter MI is substantially higher (0.47 nats). Attribution analysis, defined as the proportion of total MI attributable to source versus filter components, reveals source dominance for Emotional dimensions (80%) and filter dominance for Linguistic and Pathological dimensions (60% and 58%). These findings provide a principled framework for quantifying dimensional independence in speech.

items.title: Speaker Identity in Non-Verbal Vocalizations: Conditional Distillation and Mixture of Experts Approach
items.authors: Tzu-Chieh Wei(University of Michigan); Yi-Cheng Lin(National Taiwan University); Huang-Cheng Chou(University of Southern California); Kuan-Yu Chen(National Taiwan University); Hsin-Yen Sung(University of Southern California); Shrikanth Narayanan(University of Southern California); Hung-yi Lee(National Taiwan University)
items.abstract: As expressive text-to-speech (TTS) and voice conversion (VC) systems increasingly generate non-verbal vocalizations (NVVs) to enhance naturalness, reliable speaker verification (SV) becomes essential to objectively assess identity consistency across both verbal and non-verbal segments. Yet current SV systems generalize poorly to NVVs, and fine-tuning on NVV data causes catastrophic forgetting of speech performance. We present the first systematic study across 10 NVV types and propose a framework combining frozen Data2Vec self-supervised features with ECAPA-TDNN, enhanced by a Mixture of Experts (MoE) module with learned domain-aware routing. A conditional distillation loss on speech inputs via a pretrained teacher retains speech-to-speech accuracy, while a contrastive loss bridges the speech-NVV domain gap. Our method reduces speech-NVV EER from 38.93% to 22.66% over a pretrained baseline, and improves speech EER from 13.17% to 9.24% via distillation.

items.title: GMOD: Voice-Face Association Learning via Graph Mining and Orthogonal Disentanglement
items.authors: Jianrong Wang(Tianjin University; Tianjin Renai College); Kaibin Bi(Tianjin University); Jinghui Li(Tianjin Renai College); Ju Zhang(Tianjin University of Technology); Qi Li(Tianjin University); Ying Guo(Tianjin University); Jing Zhao(Tianjin Beiyang Rongke Intelligent Technology Co., Ltd.)
items.abstract: Existing unsupervised voice-face association methods typically rely on clustering to mitigate false-negative conflicts but often struggle with unreliable pseudo-labels due to rigid prototype assumptions. To overcome this, we propose GMOD, a novel graph-based framework. First, we introduce a global similarity graph with a curriculum-guided mining strategy to capture fine-grained identity distributions. This enables the discovery of latent positive samples for multi-positive contrastive learning, robustly mitigating early-stage noise. Second, we design an orthogonal disentanglement mechanism to effectively extract cross-modal shared identity features, thereby enhancing identity consistency. Extensive experiments on the VoxCeleb dataset demonstrate that GMOD significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Our code and pre-trained models are available online https://github.com/BKB00001/GMOD.

items.title: Tracing the Origins: Legacy Codec Identification in Neural Audio Transcoding
items.authors: Wonje Heo(DGIST); Shinee Youn(DGIST); Yooshin Kim(DGIST); Chuck Chae(DGIST); Donghoon Shin(DGIST)
items.abstract: Residual Vector Quantization (RVQ)-based neural audio codecs (NACs) enable high-fidelity audio distribution at unprecedentedly low bitrates through discrete token-based representations. However, this shift disrupts traditional forensics, as non-linear neural transcoding obscures the underlying traces of legacy compression. This study defines the forensic gap and proposes a Transformer-based framework designed to leverage the hierarchical and temporal dependencies inherent in RVQ sequences. By modeling inter-layer causal relationships and dynamic forensic significance, our model effectively disentangles superimposed artifacts from legacy-to-neural transcoding. Experimental results achieve 97%+ accuracy for codec identification and robust joint identification performance across 32-128 kbps. These results demonstrate that traditional codec traces persist even after neural transcoding, supporting the feasibility and necessity of neural-codec-aware audio forensics.

items.title: Hamsa: A Manually Annotated Emirati Arabic Corpus for Speech and Language Technologies
items.authors: Mohammed Alyafeai(Technology and Innovation Institute); Hamza Alobeidli(Technology and Innovation Institute); Omar Alkaabi(Technology and Innovation Institute); Shaikha Alsuwaidi(Technology and Innovation Institute); Leen AlQadi(Technology and Innovation Institute); Ahmed Alzubaidi(Technology and Innovation Institute); Maitha Alhammadi(Technology and Innovation Institute); Basma El Amel Boussaha(Technology and Innovation Institute); Hakim Hacid(Technology and Innovation Institute)
items.abstract: Emirati Arabic, a widely spoken Gulf dialect, is severely underrepresented in speech resources, limiting dialectal ASR and NLP applications. We introduce Hamsa, a manually annotated Emirati Arabic speech-to-text corpus containing 11 hours of conversational recordings across multiple emirates. All speech was transcribed and validated by native speakers, capturing natural pronunciation and regional variation. Challenges included informal speech, dialectal diversity, and background noise. We fine-tuned state-of-the-art multilingual Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) models on Hamsa and achieved significant performance improvements, with Word Error Rates reducing from over 40% to below 25% for Whisper-v2. Hamsa enables dialect-aware ASR, machine translation, automatic subtitling, LLM training, and commercial applications, such as call center automation, filling a critical gap in Emirati Arabic annotated speech resources.

items.title: Sub-band Cepstral Analysis of Speaker-Specific Information: A Case Study of Japanese Word /saN/
items.authors: Shunichi Ishihara(Australian National University); Frantz Clermont(Australian National University); Can Zhang(Australian National University)
items.abstract: This study applies band limited cepstral coefficients (BLCCs) to forensic voice comparison (FVC) to identify speaker-sensitive spectral regions for the Japanese fricative /s/, vowel /a/, and nasal /N/ produced by 306 male speakers. Derived from full band cepstral coefficients via linear transformation, BLCCs allow flexible extraction of sub-band information without re-analysing the signal. Using 0.6-kHz sub-bands shifted in 0.2-kHz increments across 0–8 kHz, FVC experiments were run for each segment. The vowel /a/ and nasal /N/ outperformed the fricative /s/, and all segments showed weak speaker information in the 7–8 kHz region. Speaker-sensitive sub-bands varied across segments and were not always predictable from their articulatory or acoustic characteristics. The findings also demonstrate the effectiveness of the BLCC method in accessing and analysing any local spectral region of interest.

items.title: Hybrid Continual Learning for Low-Resource Australian Aboriginal Language Identification
items.authors: Pravina Mylvaganam(University of New South Wales); Ting Dang(University of Melbourne); Eliathamby Ambikairajah(University of New South Wales); Vidhyasaharan Sethu(University of New South Wales); Jingyao Wu(Massachusetts Institute of Technology)
items.abstract: Language identification is an important step toward integrating endangered Australian Aboriginal languages (AALs) into speech technologies supporting language revitalisation and digital inclusion. However, extreme data scarcity limits model performance. Transfer learning from high-resource languages shows promise but often suffers from catastrophic forgetting when adapting to new languages. Continual learning (CL) can mitigate this issue, though it remains challenging with very limited data. To address this, we propose two hybrid continual learning methods: Replay Augmented Elastic Weight Consolidation and Constraint-Guided Knowledge Distillation to adapt pretrained speech models for AAL identification while preserving previously learned knowledge. Experiments on Warlpiri, Dalabon and Dharawal show that the proposed methods outperform fine-tuning and existing CL baselines, improving adaptation to multiple AALs while maintaining performance on previously learnt high-resource languages.
